newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan left rages as Aleman inauguration nears.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan left rages as Aleman inauguration nears.

text.p: Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega on Wednesday urged Nicaraguans to protest a Supreme Court decision wiping out dozens of Sandinista-backed laws.

Ortega, speaking in the final session of the outgoing National Assembly, called the Supreme Court ruling "a death sentence for the rule of law in Nicaragua" and said his party would accept even violent protest to defend the stricken laws.
The Supreme Court's ruling and Ortega's reaction, have sparked fears of instability in Nicaragua, as President-elect Arnoldo Aleman, the Sandinistas' bitter enemy, prepared to assume power on Friday.
The Sandinistas have a history of revolutionary militancy and often used their muscle to frustrate the early years of the outgoing government of President Violeta Chamorro.

Jubilant Liberals congratulated the Supreme Court for striking down laws they said were illegally passed by the parliament to tie the hands of the incoming government and award cushy jobs to outgoing legislators.

"Nicaraguans must do whatever is needed to raise the flag of the rule of law. We have already fought dictatorships, and now we are ready to fight this aggression using whatever it takes," said Ortega, a former president who headed Nicaragua's 1979-1990 revolutionary Sandinista government.

The Supreme Court late on Tuesday struck down dozens of laws passed by the Sandinistas and their allies in the National Assembly in recent weeks in sessions that were boycotted by pro-Aleman legislators.

Ortega accused the Supreme Court, Chamorro and the incoming Aleman government of conspiring to strike down the laws and "break the constitutional order" and called for the removal of Supreme Court magistrates.

"The court's decision puts the country in a crisis situation that I estimate will scare away foreign investors for at least a year," said outgoing congressman Alfredo Cesar, whose election as Central Bank president was one of the measures struck down by the court.

Ortega would not say whether protests were planned for Aleman's inauguration on Friday, expected to be attended by seven presidents and delegations from 61 countries as well as an estimated 22,000 spectators.
Officials have redoubled security, deploying 2,300 police officers around Managua's Rigoberto Lopez Perez Stadium, site of Aleman's inauguration, and in key plazas and hotels.

Aleman, the portly former mayor of Managua, takes power amid high hopes and predictions of soaring economic growth. But tough challenges remain. He inherits the second-poorest country in Latin America, still haunted by a bitter right-left polarization and chronic unemployment.
